accuracy.evidence: Definitions checked against CCSS RL.4.6 and standard terminology (first person, third-person limited and omniscient; narrator distinct from author). Every SPOT sentence was checked by hand: pronouns inside speech marks do not set the narration; 'My brother grabbed the map before I could stop him' is first person despite being about him. The retell keeps quoted 'me' unchanged, which is correct convention.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented errors: labelling any sentence with I as first person even inside dialogue (step 0 prediction, Tom card, Leo challenge), believing a first-person narrator knows others' thoughts (minds step), changing pronouns inside speech when retelling (step 2 prediction and quoted words that refuse to change), half-changed sentences mixing narrators (Kim challenge), and thinking two tellings of an event must match.

lab_distinct.evidence: Mechanisms belong to point of view: a narrator switch that decides whose thought bubbles open (Ella's only, or all three), word tiles that must be swapped I→Ella, my→her while grey speech-mark tiles refuse, and two tellings of one smashed window whose details are sorted by teller. Lab gate similarity under 30% to every other flag lab, including the existing narrative-perspective and point-of-view labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: Learners discover the rule through blocked actions: Ben's and Grandma's minds stay shut with Ella narrating and only outward signs appear; quoted words will not change; Sam's version lacks the running off while Mrs Patel's lacks the wind. The text confirms each finding after it happens.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions with tempting wrong options the lab disproves: 'Tom, first person: it says I', 'Yes, a first-person narrator is telling the story so knows', 'every me changes', 'same event so same details'.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with tagged distractors and specific messages: quote (the I is Leo's speech), nobody (every story has a narrator), mind (one narrator cannot read others), swap (me is the narrator, so Jess is someone else), all and always (why choose first vs third), liar and oneway (different details are choices, not lies), half (both narrator words must change).

readability.evidence: Kid text FK grade 4.1 and adult 6.7 (limits 6.5 and 9.5). Terms first person, third person and narrator are each explained in a short sentence with the pronouns that signal them.

no_filler.evidence: Filler gate passed. Each kid paragraph does one job: what a narrator is, first person and its limit, third person and the speech-mark trap, how the narrator shapes the story and why authors choose. Explanation is under 12% similar to lessons 212 and 258.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 and desktop screenshots of every step after Show me (/workspace/wn-run-1116-1146/.tmp_run/shots, pv-*). Narrator switch cards are half-width 48 px; the three character panels keep thought bubbles readable at 11 px with wrapping; word tiles are 46 px tall at 18 px text; the two tellings stack full-width on a phone above the card and boxes. Every action has a button.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs passed on desktop and iPhone 13: all five tasks complete with Show me, challenge shown, axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in light and dark themes, no console errors. The canvas aria-label reads both tellings in full on the compare step, the current card and boxes, the narrator and minds tried, or the sentence as retold so far.
